strengths: OneCAT provides a useful integration of encoder-free visual understanding, next-scale image generation, and reference-conditioned editing within a shared transformer. Modality-specific FFNs with shared attention offer a coherent way to combine continuous image inputs and discrete generative representations.

The empirical evaluation covers 12 understanding benchmarks, two generation benchmarks, and an editing benchmark. OneCAT-3B reports strong results, including 0.90 GenEval without prompt rewriting, 84.53 DPG-Bench, and 3.43 ImgEdit. These demonstrate competitive unified capabilities without requiring superiority on every benchmark.

Understanding performance is strong relative to the reported encoder-free baselines: OneCAT-3B achieves 81.2 ChartQA, 91.2 DocVQA, 52.2 MM-Vet, and 61.7 MathVista. The two model sizes also provide evidence that the approach works beyond a single configuration.

The reported efficiency improvements are practically meaningful. On one H800, Table 8 reports 50.4–61.4% lower TTFT than Qwen2.5-VL-3B, while Table 9 reports 1024×1024 generation and editing in 2.85 and 4.61 seconds. The training-stage descriptions, data-source summaries, and hyperparameter table provide useful implementation context.
weaknesses: The central limitation is the complete absence of controlled ablations. There is no comparison without scale-aware adapters, without understanding distillation, with shared versus specialized FFNs, or with separate versus joint task training. Consequently, the manuscript establishes a capable complete system but does not establish the benefit of its principal new component or the claimed cross-task synergy. This is especially consequential because the system combines established encoder-free modeling and VAR/Infinity mechanisms with extensive curated and synthetic training data. The strong system results and this unresolved attribution place my recommendation at the decision boundary.

The efficiency measurements support the reported configurations, but their general interpretation is underdetermined. Table 9 compares different backbone sizes and omits BAGEL's sampling-step count, guidance settings, precision, batching, and implementation details. No quality-versus-latency curve or next-scale generation baseline is provided. Thus, the approximately 10× advantage cannot be attributed entirely to the proposed architecture.

Reproduction of the generation method remains difficult. The manuscript does not sufficiently specify positional encoding, exact scale schedules, construction and shifting of next-scale inputs and targets, or bitwise prediction and sampling settings. These details matter because within-scale attention must operate on appropriately constructed inputs during teacher forcing. Substantial in-house instruction and synthetic datasets also lack detailed construction recipes, and the supplied manuscript contains no usable code or checkpoint link.

Several headline claims exceed the evidence. The abstract's broad superiority claim is inconsistent with Show-o2's higher DPG-Bench score (86.14 versus 84.53), OmniGen2's slightly higher editing score (3.44 versus 3.43), and stronger unified-model results on some understanding benchmarks. Small generation-score differences are reported without uncertainty estimates. These qualifications would not diminish the value of the competitive results.

Architectural terminology needs greater precision. Training includes feature-level MSE distillation in addition to autoregressive losses, despite the 'single autoregressive objective' framing. Inference still requires Infinity's image detokenizer, so eliminating external components is broader than the implemented design. Claims that learned patch embeddings are lossless or near-lossless are also unsupported by reconstruction evidence or an invertibility argument.

strengths: OneCAT provides a useful architectural integration: raw-image patch inputs, modality-specific FFNs, and next-scale image generation share one attention backbone. Supporting understanding, generation, and reference-image editing without an inference-time vision encoder is a meaningful systems contribution, even though several ingredients build on prior work.

The evaluation demonstrates substantial capability across all three tasks. OneCAT-3B achieves 0.90 on GenEval without prompt rewriting, 84.53 on DPG-Bench, and 3.43 on ImgEdit-Bench (Tables 5–7). These results support competitive unified modeling rather than merely a proof of concept.

Understanding evaluation is broad, covering 12 benchmarks. Tables 3–4 show strong results relative to the listed encoder-free models, including 81.2 ChartQA, 91.2 DocVQA, and 61.7 MathVista, while retaining image generation and editing capabilities.

The reported latency improvements have practical value: Table 8 shows 50.4–61.4% lower TTFT than Qwen2.5-VL-3B, and Table 9 reports 2.85-second generation and 4.61-second editing at 1024×1024 on an H800. Taken together with the quality results, the demonstrated system provides a stronger case for acceptance than rejection, despite the experimental reservations below.
weaknesses: The paper contains no controlled component ablations. In particular, it does not establish the benefit of the proposed scale-aware adapters, feature distillation, three-expert separation, or joint training. Given the substantial training corpus and synthetic supervision from FLUX and GPT-4o, comparisons against independently trained systems cannot isolate the architectural contributions. This materially limits the explanatory value of the work.

The efficiency experiments do not fully substantiate the claimed architectural causality. The generation comparison uses only BAGEL-7B, which differs in model size and generation mechanism. Sampling steps, CFG settings, precision, batch size, implementation optimizations, and timing variability are not specified sufficiently. The measurements support a promising system-level speed advantage, but not a controlled quality–latency advantage attributable specifically to the proposed design.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite useful training tables. The manuscript does not specify the exact multiscale schedules, positional encoding for variable-resolution inputs, scale-adapter equations, or inference sampling settings. Substantial in-house instruction and synthetic datasets are described without enough construction detail to reproduce them. The open-source claim is not accompanied by an accessible implementation or checkpoint reference in the supplied manuscript.

Several claims exceed the evidence. The abstract claims superiority across understanding, generation, and editing, but OneCAT trails Show-o2 on DPG-Bench (84.53 versus 86.14), OmniGen2 on overall editing (3.43 versus 3.44), and multiple models on understanding benchmarks. The small GenEval advantage over Mogao also lacks uncertainty estimates. Competitive overall performance is supported; universal superiority is not.

Architectural terminology needs greater precision. Image generation still requires Infinity’s pretrained VAE detokenizer, and pretraining includes an auxiliary feature-distillation loss, so the claims of a pure decoder-only system trained with a single AR objective require qualification. Likewise, the claimed lossless or near-lossless patch representation is not demonstrated. These are primarily framing issues rather than evidence that the implemented model is technically invalid.

strengths: OneCAT offers a useful architectural integration: raw-image patch embeddings, modality-specific FFNs with shared attention, and next-scale image generation jointly support understanding, generation, and editing. Bringing these capabilities into one autoregressive backbone is a worthwhile systems contribution, even though several ingredients derive from prior work.

The evaluation demonstrates substantial capability across tasks and two model sizes. OneCAT-3B achieves 0.90 on GenEval without prompt rewriting, 84.53 on DPG-Bench, and 3.43 on ImgEdit-Bench. These results establish competitive generation and editing performance without requiring leadership on every benchmark.

Understanding results are also strong, particularly against the listed encoder-free baselines. Tables 3–4 report 81.2 ChartQA, 91.2 DocVQA, and 61.7 MathVista, supporting the practical viability of combining visual understanding with image generation.

The reported efficiency gains are practically meaningful. On one H800, Tables 8–9 show 61.4% lower high-resolution input TTFT than Qwen2.5-VL-3B, and 1024×1024 generation/editing times of 2.85/4.61 seconds versus BAGEL's 26.29/46.44 seconds. The staged training recipe, dataset descriptions, and hyperparameter tables provide useful implementation context.
weaknesses: The principal scientific limitation is the absence of component ablations. There is no controlled evaluation of the proposed scale-aware adapters, understanding distillation, separate modality experts, or joint versus task-specific training. Consequently, the experiments establish the complete system's capabilities but do not establish the claimed benefits of its novel components or cross-task synergy. This matters particularly because the system also uses extensive curated and synthetic training data.

The efficiency experiments support measured system-level advantages, but attribution and reproducibility remain limited. The generation comparison changes both architecture and active model size, while sampling steps, CFG settings, precision, batch size, and implementation settings are unspecified. There is no quality–latency comparison across sampling budgets or comparison with another next-scale generator. Thus the approximately 10× speedup cannot be attributed solely to architectural unification.

Several consequential implementation details are missing: the exact next-scale input/target construction, positional encoding across native resolutions and scales, the scale schedules, and the adapter equations and placement. The manuscript also omits inference guidance values and detailed evaluation configurations. Substantial in-house datasets are described only broadly, and the supplied manuscript provides no usable code or model link despite calling the system open-source.

The originality is primarily in integration rather than the underlying paradigms: encoder-free modality experts, next-scale generation, and low-rank adapters have clear predecessors acknowledged in the paper. Without ablations or a closely matched architectural baseline, the incremental contribution of the scale-aware adapter—the most explicit new module—remains uncertain.

Some claims exceed the evidence and should be narrowed. The model retains an external VAE image decoder at inference, and pretraining includes an auxiliary distillation loss, qualifying the 'pure decoder-only' and 'single AR objective' descriptions. Calling the learned patch representation lossless is unsupported. The broad claim of outperforming existing unified models also overlooks Show-o2's higher DPG-Bench score, OmniGen2's slightly higher editing score, and several stronger understanding results. These wording issues are secondary to the experimental gaps. Overall, the strong demonstrated system merits serious consideration, but missing component validation and incomplete efficiency/reproduction details place the submission near the acceptance boundary.

strengths: OneCAT provides a useful architectural contribution: a shared decoder combines encoder-free visual understanding, next-scale image generation, and reference-image editing through modality-specific FFNs. Although the components build on prior work, their integration demonstrates a credible and practically relevant alternative to encoder-plus-diffusion systems.

The evaluation supports strong capabilities across all three tasks. OneCAT-3B achieves 0.90 GenEval without prompt rewriting, 84.53 DPG-Bench, and 3.43 ImgEdit-Bench (Tables 5–7), alongside competitive understanding results including 81.2 ChartQA and 91.2 DocVQA. Acceptance does not depend on being best on every benchmark.

The distillation proposal has meaningful experimental support. Full-layer matching improves the reported understanding average from 31.4 to 35.3 and exceeds the adapted EvE and VoRA strategies (Table 9). Appendix C extends this evidence across training budgets, with improvements persisting at 70B tokens.

The scale-aware adapter improves GenEval from 78.1 to 81.2 and DPG-Bench from 74.0 to 74.9 under the stated matched training-token setup (Table 12). The task-mixture experiments also indicate that adding generation training preserves understanding performance reasonably well.

The reported latency results are practically promising: on one H800, high-resolution understanding TTFT decreases from 0.583 to 0.225 seconds relative to Qwen2.5-VL-3B, and 1024-square generation takes 2.85 seconds. Together with the broad task results, these findings favor weak acceptance despite the qualifications below.
weaknesses: The efficiency evidence does not fully isolate the architectural advantage. Table 8 compares generation against a larger active-parameter BAGEL model without specifying its sampling steps, precision, batching, or implementation settings. No latency comparison to another next-scale generator is provided. The measurements support a useful system-level speed advantage under the tested setup, but not a general claim of superiority over diffusion or an attribution of the full gain to removing encoders.

The ablations only partially establish the proposed mechanisms. Removing SAA also removes parameters; there is no parameter-matched shared-adapter control to isolate scale specialization. There is also no direct ablation of the three-expert arrangement. Appendix C's randomly initialized InternViT comparison addresses a restricted training setting rather than the practical alternative of using a pretrained encoder.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful training tables and scale schedules. The manuscript does not adequately specify positional encoding across native-resolution inputs and generation scales, the exact construction of decoder inputs for next-scale prediction, or sampling settings beyond CFG. Substantial in-house synthetic data are used without sufficiently detailed generation and filtering recipes.

The broad state-of-the-art wording exceeds the reported evidence. Show-o2 scores higher on DPG-Bench (86.14 versus 84.53), OmniGen2 slightly exceeds the editing overall score (3.44 versus 3.43), and several understanding benchmarks favor other unified models. The small GenEval lead over Mogao, 0.90 versus 0.89, lacks uncertainty estimates. The supported conclusion is strong, competitive performance across tasks.

Some architectural descriptions need qualification rather than indicating fundamental technical failure. Image synthesis still uses an external VAE detokenizer, and the claimed lossless or near-lossless patch representation is not established through reconstruction or information-preservation evidence. Likewise, retaining language ability is a stated training objective but is not evaluated on text-only tasks.

strengths: OneCAT makes a useful architectural contribution by combining encoder-free visual understanding, next-scale image generation, and image editing within one decoder backbone. Although its ingredients build on existing work, their integration demonstrates a credible alternative to unified models using separate vision encoders and diffusion components.

Evaluation spans 13 understanding benchmarks, two generation benchmarks, and image editing. OneCAT-3B achieves 0.90 GenEval without prompt rewriting, 84.53 DPG-Bench, and 3.43 ImgEdit-Bench, alongside strong understanding results such as 81.2 ChartQA and 91.2 DocVQA. This supports broad practical capability rather than success on one selected task.

Table 8 reports substantial practical speed advantages on a common H800: 0.225 versus 0.583 seconds for high-resolution understanding prefill, and 2.85 versus 26.29 seconds for 1024-pixel generation against BAGEL. These measurements make the architectural direction potentially valuable even without uniformly best benchmark accuracy.

The ablations provide meaningful support for two proposed components. Full-layer distillation improves the reported understanding average from 31.4 to 35.3, outperforming the tested alternative distillation strategies. Scale-aware adapters improve GenEval from 78.1 to 81.2 and DPG from 74.0 to 74.9. Together with the broad end-to-end results, this evidence favors acceptance despite the reservations below.
weaknesses: The efficiency comparison does not isolate architectural causes. Generation compares a 3B-active model against BAGEL-7B without specifying BAGEL's sampling steps, precision, batch size, or implementation settings. No quality–latency sweep is provided. Thus, the reported speedups support these particular configurations, but not a general tenfold advantage over diffusion-based methods.

The architectural ablations leave important attribution questions unresolved. Removing SAA also removes parameters; there is no parameter-matched shared-adapter control establishing the benefit of scale specialization itself. Modality-specific FFNs are not compared against a shared-FFN alternative, and most component ablations use the smaller model with simplified training rather than the final recipe.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite useful hyperparameter tables and scale schedules. Training relies heavily on in-house synthetic data, including 30 million FLUX-generated images, without sufficient generation and filtering details to reconstruct the mixture. Positional encoding and the precise construction of next-scale decoder inputs are also insufficiently specified for reproducing the unified architecture.

Several claims exceed the evidence. OneCAT trails Show-o2 on DPG-Bench (84.53 versus 86.14) and MMMU (41.9 versus 48.9), while its editing score is slightly below OmniGen2. Small leading margins, such as 0.90 versus 0.89 GenEval, lack uncertainty estimates. The results establish strong competitiveness, not uniform superiority across unified models.

Some conceptual language needs qualification. The model retains an external VAE image detokenizer, and the learned patch embedding is not demonstrated to be lossless or near-lossless. Appendix C finds broadly comparable early- and late-fusion accuracy without distillation, rather than intrinsic superiority of early fusion. These are primarily claim-calibration issues, but they obscure what the experiments actually establish.

strengths: OneCAT makes a useful architectural contribution by integrating encoder-free visual understanding, next-scale image generation, and editing in one decoder with modality-specific FFNs. Although several ingredients build on prior work, their integration provides a credible and practically relevant unified model.

Evaluation spans diverse understanding benchmarks, compositional generation, and instruction-based editing. OneCAT-3B achieves 0.90 GenEval without prompt rewriting, 84.53 DPG-Bench, and 3.43 ImgEdit-Bench, alongside strong understanding results such as 81.2 ChartQA and 91.2 DocVQA. This supports broad capability rather than a gain on one benchmark.

The ablations provide meaningful support for two proposed components. Full-layer teacher distillation improves the average understanding score from 31.4 to 35.3 and exceeds the tested EvE and VoRA strategies (Table 9). Scale-aware adapters improve GenEval from 78.1 to 81.2 and DPG from 74.0 to 74.9 (Table 12).

The reported efficiency gains are practically significant: Table 8 measures 0.225-second versus 0.583-second understanding TTFT at high resolution, and 2.85-second versus 26.29-second generation at 1024×1024 on one H800. These measurements support the usefulness of the design, subject to the comparison limitations below.

The training stages, token budgets, task ratios, distillation objective, guidance settings, and resolution schedules are substantially documented. Overall, the demonstrated breadth, component-level evidence, and promising efficiency favor acceptance despite reservations about causal attribution and reproducibility.
weaknesses: Architectural attribution remains incomplete. There is no controlled ablation of the three-expert design against shared FFNs, and the SAA comparison lacks a parameter-matched shared-adapter baseline. It therefore establishes that SAA helps, but does not isolate scale specialization from added capacity. Most component ablations also use reduced-budget 1.5B models rather than the final 3B setting.

The approximately 10× generation speedup is a system comparison against a larger BAGEL model, not an isolated estimate of the benefit of autoregression or encoder removal. Table 8 omits important timing settings, including BAGEL sampling steps, precision, batching, and implementation optimizations. A quality–latency comparison and runtime breakdown would make the central efficiency claim more convincing.

The broad state-of-the-art language exceeds the evidence. Show-o2-7B scores higher on DPG-Bench (86.14 versus 84.53), OmniGen2 slightly exceeds the overall editing score, and several unified models outperform OneCAT on individual understanding benchmarks. BAGEL and Mogao are absent from the understanding comparisons despite being central unified-model competitors. These qualifications do not negate the strong results, but narrow the supported superiority claim.

Reproduction depends on incompletely specified data construction, including 30 million in-house FLUX images and additional synthetic instruction and SFT data. Filtering thresholds, synthesis recipes, and benchmark-overlap checks are not sufficiently documented. The manuscript also provides no usable project link or available implementation, leaving substantial uncertainty about reproducing the full training pipeline.

Some explanatory claims need greater precision. Patch embedding is described as lossless or near-lossless without reconstruction evidence, and eliminating external components should be qualified because image synthesis still uses a pretrained VAE detokenizer. Small benchmark margins are also reported without uncertainty estimates, so they should not be treated as decisive improvements.
